title: Session timeout is admin-configurable idle-disconnect policy
detail: Kiteworks platform enables system administrators to set session timeout policies that disconnect users after a defined period of inactivity. No default value published; it is a per-deployment setting. Implication: the hunting env's timeout is whatever the program operator configured — timeout behavior must be measured, not assumed.
evidence: Kiteworks CMMC 2.0 compliance mapping (kiteworks.com): 'enables system administrators to set session timeout policies, disconnecting users after a defined period of inactivity'

title: 'Remember this device' trusted-device mechanism can bypass 2FA step
detail: Sign-in screen offers a 'Remember this device' checkbox that temporarily registers the computer/phone as a trusted device, letting the user skip the 2FA passcode on subsequent sign-ins. Admin-controlled whether allowed. This is the remember-me equivalent: a persistent trust token exists client-side.
evidence: Kiteworks Getting Started Guide p.7 (multiple mirrors incl. sca.gdit.com, global.mftservice.com)

title: Sign-out is explicit UI action; SSO deployments wire Single Logout
detail: Standard sign-out: username (upper right) -> Sign Out. SEC deployment guide describes a dedicated Logout tab. SSO setups (documented for Microsoft Entra ID) configure a Single Logout Service URL, i.e. IdP-initiated logout is supported.
evidence: Kiteworks Getting Started Guide; SEC 'External Guide for Using Kiteworks'; Microsoft Entra Kiteworks SSO tutorial (learn.microsoft.com)

title: 2FA is 8-digit email OTP with 5-minute expiry; MFA enforceable per admin session
detail: Two-factor uses an 8-digit one-time passcode sent by email, expiring in 5 minutes. Platform can be configured to require MFA for any administrative session, and to time out those sessions after an idle threshold (replay resistance). Alternative: SMS passcodes, RADIUS, PIV/CAC cards.
evidence: SEC 'What is KiteWorks?' guide (OTP 8-digit, 5-min expiry); Kiteworks CMMC 2.0 mapping IA.L2-3.5.4

title: Failed-login account lockout is admin-configured with email notification
detail: After N incorrect passwords (threshold and lockout duration set by admin), the account locks and the user is notified by email; may also trigger CAPTCHA challenges before lockout. Relevant to session research: lockout state is server-side per account.
evidence: Kiteworks Getting Started Guide p.7

title: API auth is token-based, separate from web session cookies
detail: REST API supports: API Key auth (Authorization: Bearer <api_key>) for server-to-server; OAuth 2.0 (Bearer <access_token>) for user delegation with refresh-token rotation; mutual TLS client certs. Legacy Accellion-style flow used HMAC-SHA1 signature auth codes with X-Accellion-Version header and scopes like */files/*. Web UI session cookies and API tokens are distinct credential types.
evidence: kiteworks.com API-Driven MFT Integration Guide; legacy Kiteworks admin guide (watoniworawi.weebly.com mirror)

title: Concurrent-session policy not found in public docs — open question
detail: No public Kiteworks documentation found describing concurrent-session limits, session listing/revocation UI, or 'log out other devices'. This is unverified territory for the manual phase: check whether the profile/settings area exposes active sessions.
evidence: Multiple doc searches (admin guides, getting-started, CMMC mappings) returned no concurrent-session policy

title: Three-layer privilege model: user profiles, admin roles, folder roles
detail: Kiteworks separates privileges into three layers: (1) user profiles — the feature/privilege container assigned to every user; (2) admin roles — 8 default + custom delegated roles with configurable component scope governing administrative functions; (3) folder roles — Owner, Manager, Collaborator, Downloader, Uploader, Viewer governing data access. A role transition can occur at any of the three layers, and a flaw in one layer's transition guard does not imply the others are guarded.
evidence: github.com/kiteworks/mcp AVAILABLE_TOOLS.md (Admin User Profiles tools); kiteworks.com Defence Standard 05-138 guide (8 default admin roles, delegated roles, separation of duties); Kiteworks Packaging/Licensing doc (folder roles list)

title: Users start with zero privileges; privileges come only from assigned user profile
detail: Per Kiteworks' Defence Standard compliance guide, 'all users initially have no privileges and only receive privileges for functionality when assigned a user profile', and data-access privileges arrive 'only by invitation from users who manage the data'. The user profile is therefore the single choke point for privilege grants — whoever controls profile assignment controls privilege escalation.
evidence: kiteworks.com Defence Standard 05-138 guide, control 2205 (Least privilege)

title: assign_user_profile is the promotion/demotion primitive, gated behind Admin READ scope
detail: The official Kiteworks MCP server docs list 'assign_user_profile: Assign a single user to a profile (promotion or demotion)' and 'bulk_assign_profile: Assign one or more users to a profile in bulk, with data-retention controls for demotions'. The DEPLOYMENT_GUIDE scope table shows Admin READ scope enables 'Admin user tools, shared mailboxes, admin activity, list_user_profiles, assign_user_profile' while Admin CREATE enables 'create_user only'. So profile promotion requires Admin READ — the exact authorization boundary to probe is whether delegated/limited admins are correctly scoped out of this call.
evidence: github.com/kiteworks/mcp docs/AVAILABLE_TOOLS.md and docs/DEPLOYMENT_GUIDE.md (scope table)

title: create_user endpoint strips admin role server-side (documented anti-escalation guard)
detail: The MCP deployment guide states: 'create_user cannot create administrators in any case, because the Kiteworks API ignores an admin role on that endpoint.' This is an explicit server-side guard against privilege escalation at account creation. Open question: is the strip enforced on ALL user-creation paths (SSO Just-In-Time provisioning, LDAP sync, bulk import, self-registration) or only the REST create_user endpoint?
evidence: github.com/kiteworks/mcp docs/DEPLOYMENT_GUIDE.md

title: Delegated admin roles with configurable component scope; admin role CRUD exists
detail: Kiteworks supports 'delegated admin roles with configurable component scope, supporting admin role CRUD operations (add/delete/rename) and editing of admin permissions and role components for delegated administration'. Separation of duties is enforced via distinct roles including 'builtin system admin, helpdesk admin, and custom defined roles'. The existence of role-component editing by delegated admins is the highest-risk transition surface: the guard that must hold is that a delegated admin cannot expand their own role's component scope.
evidence: kiteworks.com Defence Standard 05-138 guide, control 2203 (Privileged user management)

title: Two-tier admin hierarchy: only system admins can create application admins
detail: The Kiteworks admin guide documents the /adminRoles REST API for managing administrator-role assignment: it requires authentication as an administrative user, and 'only system administrators can [promote] users to ... application administrators. Users cannot promote themselves to system administrators.' So there is a system-admin > application-admin hierarchy, with self-promotion explicitly called out as blocked — the enforcement point (per-endpoint server check vs UI-only) is what needs manual verification.
evidence: Kiteworks admin guide (REST API section: /profiles, /roles, /adminRoles)

title: Profile mapping rules auto-assign profiles by matching username/email
detail: The admin toolkit exposes 'get_profile_eligibility: Test profile mapping rules against a username/email and see which would match'. Profile assignment can therefore happen automatically via rules, not just manual admin action. Any flow that lets a user change the attributes rules match on (e.g., email change) or lets an admin edit the rules is a role-transition path that bypasses the assign_user_profile authorization check entirely.
evidence: github.com/kiteworks/mcp docs/AVAILABLE_TOOLS.md (Admin - User Profiles)

title: update_user excludes profile from mutable fields; role changes are funneled through assign_user_profile
detail: Per the MCP docs, 'update_user: Update mutable fields on a user (name, password, suspended, verified, deactivated, active)' — profile/adminRole are NOT in the mutable list. By design, privilege changes must go through assign_user_profile, not the generic user-update endpoint. The manual test is whether the underlying REST API actually rejects a profile/adminRole parameter on the user-update path (mass-assignment probe) or merely omits it from docs.
evidence: github.com/kiteworks/mcp docs/AVAILABLE_TOOLS.md (Admin - User Management)

title: Scope-naming mismatch: read-only profile tools require Profiles CREATE scope
detail: The deployment guide notes 'the read-only profile tools (get_profile, list_profile_users, get_profile_eligibility) need Profiles CREATE, because that is the scope the Kiteworks API enforces on those endpoints.' A read operation gated behind a CREATE scope suggests the authorization model grew organically; scope/endpoint mismatches are where over-permissive grants hide. Worth mapping exactly which endpoints check which scope.
evidence: github.com/kiteworks/mcp docs/DEPLOYMENT_GUIDE.md

title: H1: Delegated admin invokes assign_user_profile outside their component scope
detail: If assign_user_profile checks only 'has Admin READ' and not the delegated admin's component scope, a limited delegated admin (e.g., helpdesk) could promote any user — including themselves — to a privileged profile. MANUAL TEST (human operator, low rate): with a delegated-admin test account, call the profile-assign endpoint for a target outside the delegated scope and observe allow/deny. Falsifier: server returns 403 and no profile change occurs.
evidence: Scope table grants assign_user_profile under broad Admin READ; delegated roles have 'configurable component scope' per Defence Standard guide — interaction of the two is undocumented

title: H2: Profile mapping rule manipulation yields self-promotion
detail: If profile mapping rules match on user-controlled attributes (email, display name) and are re-evaluated on attribute change, a user could engineer a match against a privileged profile's rule. Alternatively, a delegated admin able to edit mapping rules could add a rule matching their own account. MANUAL TEST: inspect rule definitions (get_profile_eligibility), attempt attribute change, re-test eligibility. Falsifier: rules match only on immutable attributes (e.g., LDAP DN) and rule editing requires system admin.
evidence: get_profile_eligibility tool exists; rule match criteria undocumented in public sources

title: H3: Delegated admin expands own role via admin role CRUD
detail: Admin role CRUD (add/delete/rename roles, edit permissions/components) exists for delegated administration. If a delegated admin holds role-edit permission, they may be able to add privileged components to their OWN role — a within-tier vertical escalation that no 'assign_user_profile' check would catch, because the role definition itself changed. MANUAL TEST: with delegated admin, attempt to add a component to own role. Falsifier: role edits require system admin, or self-edit is blocked.
evidence: Defence Standard guide documents admin role CRUD and component editing for delegated administration; self-edit guard undocumented

title: H4: Mass assignment of profile/adminRole on the user-update path
detail: update_user documents only non-privilege fields as mutable, but the underlying REST endpoint may still bind a 'profile' or admin-role parameter if supplied. MANUAL TEST: as an admin, submit user-update with an added profile parameter for a test user and check whether the profile changed. Falsifier: parameter ignored / 400, profile unchanged.
evidence: Mutable-field list is documentation-level; server-side binding behavior unverified

title: H5: Demotion does not revoke active sessions/tokens promptly
detail: bulk_assign_profile handles demotions with 'data-retention controls', which suggests demotion is a heavyweight operation. If session invalidation on demotion is asynchronous or absent, a demoted admin retains privileged access until session expiry — a time-of-check/time-of-use gap in the role transition. MANUAL TEST: demote a test admin, then immediately reuse their session token against an admin endpoint. Falsifier: 401/403 immediately after demotion.
evidence: Demotion called out as needing 'data-retention controls'; session-revocation-on-demotion undocumented

title: H6: create_user admin-strip bypass via SSO JIT or LDAP sync paths
detail: The documented guard ('API ignores an admin role on create_user') covers the REST endpoint. But Kiteworks supports SP-initiated SSO with Just-In-Time provisioning and LDAP/AD sync. If JIT/LDAP user creation maps IdP groups/claims to Kiteworks profiles or admin roles without the same strip, an attacker controlling IdP group membership (or a misconfigured mapping) could land as admin. MANUAL TEST: review JIT/LDAP provisioning config; test whether an IdP-supplied admin indicator survives provisioning. Falsifier: all provisioning paths funnel through the same guarded creation routine.
evidence: Microsoft Entra tutorial confirms Kiteworks SP-initiated SSO + JIT provisioning; admin guide confirms LDAP group integration; strip documented only for the REST endpoint

title: OAuth token lifecycle: 7 grant types, per-app configurable lifetimes, optional refresh
detail: API supports Authorization Code, Signature-based Authorization Code, Signature-based Access, User Credential, User Credential (HTTP Basic), SAML 2.0 Assertion, JWT Assertion grants. Per custom application: Access Token Lifetime and Refresh Token Lifetime are admin-configurable; 'Enable Refresh Token' is optional per app. Signature-flow auth codes valid 1 hour. Scope format is method/path wildcards, e.g. '*/activities/* */admin/* */profile/* */users/* */files/* */folders/*'. Auth state is thus per-application, per-user, per-scope — token lifetime policy is not global.
evidence: Official Accellion API Guide (kiteworks.com/sites/default/api/): Custom Applications section (Flows, Enable Refresh Token, Access/Refresh Token Lifetime), 'Obtaining a Token' (7 grant types), signature flow ('code will remain valid for an hour'), scope example 'folders/* files/* mail/*'

title: Chunked upload is a stateful session: POST initiate -> X-Accellion-Location session ID -> chunk POSTs -> 201 file
detail: POST /folders/{id}/actions/initiateUpload (or /files/{file_id}/actions/initiateUpload for new version) returns 201 with session in X-Accellion-Location header (.../rest/uploads/{id}) and body uri. GET /uploads/{id} exposes session state: userId, timestamp, totalSize, totalChunks, uploadedSize, uploadedChunks, completeOk (0 until finished; session deleted after finish), error, clientCookie, clientName, backend, replaceId. Chunks POSTed to the uri; first chunk -> 200, final chunk -> 201 with file ID in X-Accellion-Location. DELETE /uploads/{id} terminates the session. Two workflows: declared totalSize/totalChunks (server validates content at end) vs SFTP-style (lastChunk=1, NO content validation on final chunk). State lives server-side keyed by numeric session ID.
evidence: API Guide 'Chunk Upload Process Steps': upload session initialization, 'Retrieve Upload Session Data' field list, chunk upload (200 per chunk, 201 + X-Accellion-Location on last), 'Terminating Upload Session' DELETE /uploads/{id}, workflow notes on lastChunk=1 skipping validation

title: Two-stage soft delete: deleted -> permDeleted; listings filterable via ?deleted=false
detail: Folder/file entities carry both 'deleted' and 'permDeleted' boolean flags plus 'expire'. GET /rest/folders/{id}/children?deleted=false filters soft-deleted items. Deletion is therefore a state transition (visible -> soft-deleted -> permanently deleted), not immediate removal. The children endpoint's deleted filter is client-controlled, which is the exact shape where IDOR/authorization checks on 'deleted' objects get missed.
evidence: API Guide: folder entity JSON shows 'deleted': false, 'permDeleted': false, 'expire': 0; children example uses /rest/folders/$folderId/children?deleted=false

title: Offset/limit pagination with metadata envelope; orderBy parameter on listings
detail: List responses wrap in {'data': [...], 'metadata': {'total': N, 'limit': null, 'offset': 0}}. Offset-based (not cursor) pagination. Example: GET /rest/folders/top?orderBy=name%3Aasc. Offset pagination is unstable under concurrent inserts (duplicates/gaps) — relevant for enumeration consistency and for any security decision made across pages.
evidence: API Guide folder-listing example response shows metadata.total/limit/offset; request example uses orderBy=name:asc

title: API versioned per-request via X-Accellion-Version header; multiple versions served concurrently
detail: Every request carries X-Accellion-Version (examples show 8, 10, 15). Docs state several API versions are all supported simultaneously and clients should pin the latest. Concurrent versions mean: deprecated-version endpoints may have weaker validation; version parameter is client-controlled; behavior differences between versions are a differential-testing surface.
evidence: API Guide: 'There are several API versions, all of which are supported'; all examples pass X-Accellion-Version header (8/10/15)

title: File versioning state machine: same filename re-upload creates new version; replaceId tracks replacement
detail: POST /folders/{id}/actions/initiateUpload with an existing filename creates a NEW VERSION of the file rather than failing. Dedicated endpoint POST /files/{file_id}/actions/initiateUpload uploads a new version of a specific file. Upload session body includes 'replaceId' (null in example). Version history is therefore server-side state; questions: who can enumerate/revert versions, do permissions on old versions match the current file, does replaceId accept arbitrary file IDs.
evidence: API Guide: 'If you call POST /folders/{id}/actions/initiateUpload with filename that already exists in this directory, the new version of this file will be created'; version-upload endpoint documented; session JSON includes 'replaceId': null

title: Async post-upload processing: fingerprint shows 'Generating...' after 201 Created
detail: Final-chunk 201 response includes file entity with 'fingerprint': 'Generating...' — content fingerprinting/AV happens asynchronously AFTER the upload completes and the file ID is issued. There is a window where the file exists (addressable by ID, possibly downloadable/shareable) before security processing finishes. Also ?returnEntity=true toggles response shape (entity in body vs header-only X-Accellion-Location).
evidence: API Guide 'Example Response (Final chunk)' shows 'fingerprint': 'Generating...' on the created file; create-folder docs describe ?returnEntity=true behavior and X-Accellion-Location header

title: No idempotency mechanism documented; upload sessions and object creation are retry-unsafe by design
detail: The full API guide documents no Idempotency-Key or equivalent for POST/PUT actions. Combined with the stateful upload session (retry of initiateUpload with same filename = new version, not dedup), retried requests can create duplicate sessions, duplicate versions, or duplicate objects. Client-driven retry after network failure is a plausible source of unintended state.
evidence: API Guide (3275 lines) contains no mention of idempotency; upload flow explicitly creates new versions on filename collision rather than deduplicating

title: SDF/Advanced Forms approval engine = 123FormBuilder approvals (acquired Sep 2024)
detail: Kiteworks Secure Data Forms are powered by 123FormBuilder (acquired 2024-09-05). Approval workflow is configured per-form in the Approvals section: single approver or chain approval (add second approver = sequential chain). Enabling auto-creates three email templates. Approval status tracked per submission in the Submissions table.
evidence: https://www.123formbuilder.com/docs/approvals/ ; CRN acquisition report 2024-09-05

title: Approval routing: broadcast default OR conditional branching on attacker-influenced fields
detail: Two routing modes: (1) email ALL submissions to the approver (default); (2) branching rules evaluated against form field values (operators: is not/contains/does not contain, AND/OR connectors, same engine as the Rules feature). Approver email can be a fixed address OR taken from a form field the submitter fills in. Routing decisions therefore depend on submitter-controlled input.
evidence: https://www.123formbuilder.com/docs/approvals/ (Configuration section)

title: Approver-from-form-field: submitter may nominate their own approver
detail: Docs explicitly allow the approver email to be 'selected from a form field (e.g. Email address field)' filled by the submitter. Intended for 'enter your manager's email' flows, but it means approval routing can be submitter-directed by design. Open question for manual testing: does approval actually gate access to submission data, or is it status-only?
evidence: https://www.123formbuilder.com/docs/approvals/

title: Rejection semantics: one rejection kills the entire chain immediately
detail: 'The approval process will be stopped immediately when the submission entry was rejected by one person.' No quorum/override documented. Inferred submission states: pending -> approved (all chain members approve) | rejected (any single reject, terminal). No documented expiry/timeout on pending approvals in the public docs.
evidence: https://www.123formbuilder.com/docs/approvals/ (Important Notes)

title: Approvals are email-driven; approval action link/token design unknown
detail: 'Build an approval workflow on your form, add the recipients and we will email them automatically.' Approvers act via emailed links. Token format, expiry, single-use, and whether the approval endpoint requires authentication are not documented publicly — classic attack surface for manual testing (token prediction, replay, CSRF on approve/reject actions).
evidence: https://www.123formbuilder.com/docs/approvals/

title: Kiteworks Core: two-tier DPE approval for restricted file transfers
detail: Data Policy Engine intercepts transfers labeled Highly Restricted and triggers a structured chain: user initiates transfer -> DPE reads MIP label -> Stage 1 business-unit VP authorization -> Stage 2 legal team review -> transfer completes. BOTH stages must explicitly approve; no file moves until cleared. Confidential and lower pass automatically. VP notified via Outlook; approvals/denials with reasons logged to a full audit trail.
evidence: https://staging.kiteworks.com/sites/default/files/resources/kiteworks-case-study-protecting-ip-supply-chain-edge.pdf

title: Vendor access onboarding workflow: request -> approver -> MFA -> provision
detail: Documented onboarding flow: vendor submits access request through secure portal -> system routes to approver based on requested access level -> approver reviews business justification, approves/rejects -> system generates docs (NDA/BAA/attestation) -> vendor completes electronically -> identity verified via MFA -> access provisioned per approved permissions. Access-level-driven routing is the trust-critical step.
evidence: https://www.kiteworks.com/third-party-risk/third-party-file-transfer-security-strategies/

title: SDF publish/integration surface: forms render client-side, data flows to 45+ third parties
detail: Forms publish via direct URL, JS embed, inline HTML, iFrame, WordPress plugin, popups. 123FormBuilder integrates with 45+ tools (Salesforce, Stripe, HubSpot, Shopify). Post-approval data flows to third-party systems are part of the workflow; each integration is a data-exfiltration-shaped trust boundary worth mapping on the live env.
evidence: CRN 2024-09-05 acquisition report; https://www.123formbuilder.com/docs/approvals/ (FAQ publish section)

title: Folder notifications: trigger set and subscription model
detail: Emails are sent when someone uploads a file to a shared folder, adds a new file version, edits a file, comments on a file, or copies/moves a file into the folder. Notifications are opt-in per folder; owner/manager can subscribe others at invite time; batching merges rapid same-folder events into one email. Roles Owner/Manager/Collaborator/Downloader/Viewer may subscribe; Viewers cannot view file comments.
evidence: Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0 (Aug 2025), p.63 'Manage folder notification settings'

title: Download-tracking email carries filename + downloader email
detail: Sender option 'Notify me when attachments are downloaded' emails the sender a timestamped notification containing the name of the file and the email of the person who downloaded it, with an 'Also notify' field to add other users. This is a recipient-email disclosure primitive driven entirely by sender-side configuration.
evidence: Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0, p.34, Table 4 'Message settings'

title: Attachment-expiry report email lists per-recipient activity
detail: Sender option 'Notify me when attachments expire' emails a report listing the files that expired and whether recipients opened, downloaded, or copied them to a folder. Attachment links expire on the specified date at 23:59:59 UTC.
evidence: Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0, p.34, Table 4 'Message settings'

title: Subject line visible even when body is 'protected'
detail: With 'Recipients must sign in to view the message body and file attachments list' enabled, non-authenticated recipients see only the list (they must sign in to download), but the guide warns explicitly: 'Caution: The subject line will be visible to recipients.' Metadata in subjects is not protected by the message-body setting.
evidence: Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0, p.34, Table 4 'Message settings'

title: Tracking-access grant emails link and expose Bcc to trackers
detail: Granting tracking access emails non-recipients a notification with a link to open the message in the web app. Trackers see the message body, the FULL recipient list INCLUDING Bcc recipients, and can download attachments, send activity details to others, and export CSV. Tracked activity: message viewed/replied/forwarded/deleted; attachments viewed/downloaded/copied/sent.
evidence: Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0, pp.39-41 'Allow others to track message activity'

title: File-request invitation emails with configurable upload links
detail: 'Request Files' sends an email invitation containing an upload link. Requester controls per-recipient upload count and link expiry (23:59:59 UTC; a 'Link never expires' option exists until the message is withdrawn). Uploader's email address is appended to the uploaded file name for identification. 'Notify others when files are uploaded' emails other users on upload without giving them inbox access.
evidence: Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0, pp.103-106, Table 14

title: Message-to-folder-members and push-to-device emails
detail: 'Message to Members' emails each recipient a message with a secure link to sign in and access the folder (Owner/Manager/Collaborator only). 'Push File' sends each folder member an email with a link to open the file in the mobile app for offline editing (Owner/Manager only; disabled in restricted folders).
evidence: Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0, pp.107,109

title: Task assignment/edit emails carry secure links; creator copied
detail: Assigning a file task emails the assignee a description plus a secure link to the file, and the creator receives a copy. Editing a task emails the task creator about the change, with the editor receiving a copy.
evidence: Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0, pp.110-111

title: Auth-related emails: 2FA passcode, lockout, reset link, activation
detail: 2FA passcode can be delivered by email each sign-in; entering the password wrong too many times triggers an account-lockout notification email; 'Forgot Password' flow emails a password-reset link; new external users receive a confirmation email with an 'Activate Account' button before they can reach their inbox. CAPTCHA may be required after bad passwords.
evidence: Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0 p.10; Getting Started Guide; OCG NSW Accellion Kiteworks guide 2021; HBF Kiteworks user guide FAQ

title: EPG: every email event logged with rule + action + delivery outcome
detail: Email Protection Gateway applies Data Policy Engine actions (encryption, routing, quarantine, rejection) invisibly across all inbound/outbound mail based on sender/recipient/content/label/attributes. EVERY message is logged to the unified Kiteworks audit log with the rule matched, action taken, and delivery outcome, feeding SIEM. Supports S/MIME, OpenPGP, SMTP/TLS, AV/DLP/ATP attachment scanning, Microsoft RMS auto-conversion.
evidence: https://www.kiteworks.com/platform/simple/email-protection-gateway/

title: Mail API: validationId-gated send, OTP phone check, shared mailboxes
detail: The mail API (per official MCP server docs) uses a compose-then-send flow: compose_email validates against policy and, for acl=otp, verifies recipients have a phone number on file, returning a validationId; send_email transmits only the validated draft. get_mail exposes subject/body/status/AV-DLP scan status/recipients/attachments. Admin: create_user requires sendNotification; request_file_to_folder sends email invitation with upload link.
evidence: https://github.com/kiteworks/mcp/blob/HEAD/docs/AVAILABLE_TOOLS.md

title: ownCloud share mail notifications: admin-gated, owner-language
detail: Kiteworks subsidiary ownCloud: admin must enable 'Allow users to send mail notification for shared files'; admin picks the notification language via shareapi_public_notification_lang (default: share owner's language). Requires the server be configured to send mail.
evidence: https://doc.owncloud.com/server/10.15/admin_manual/configuration/files/file_sharing_configuration.html

title: Secure Data Forms: real-time policy-drift alerts to security teams
detail: Secure Data Forms 'real-time alerts notify security and compliance teams when form configurations drift from policy requirements, unusual access patterns emerge, or data moves between regions' — a notification channel triggered by compliance/policy events rather than user actions.
evidence: Kiteworks Secure Data Forms launch announcement (cebit.einnews.com, PR)

title: Research note: notification-content exposure surface for verification agents
detail: Candidate verification surface from docs alone (NOT tested on target): (a) 'Also notify' fields on download/expiry notifications as potential unauthorized-recipient-add vectors; (b) tracking-access grants exposing Bcc lists to non-recipients; (c) external-distribution-list domain-any-address access; (d) unprotected subject lines on 'protected' messages; (e) upload-link expiry/nonever-expire handling. All need authorized manual verification on the hunting env; no conclusions drawn.
evidence: Synthesized from Kiteworks Web User Guide v9.1.0 notification sections (passive OSINT only)

title: Client blindly navigates to server-returned redirectUrl (3 locations)
detail: After login (POST /rest/users/actions/login), after preauth when type==='redirect', and after OTP auth, the client runs window.location.assign(redirectUrl) with zero allowlist/origin validation (only a carve-out for '/sw/guide/'). The login request sends referral=window.location.href. If the server derives redirectUrl from the client-supplied referral, this is an open redirect. Open redirect is program-qualifying.
evidence: signin.f7b86212.js: 'if(e.redirectUrl){const{redirectUrl:t}=e;t.includes("/sw/guide/")?w(H):window.location.assign(t)}' ; preauth: 'if("redirect"===a)s&&window.location.assign(s)' ; OTP: 'else window.location.assign(n)'. Login posts {username,password,referral:window.location.href,captcha_salt,captcha_value} to /rest/users/actions/login.

title: ignoreOtp query param may downgrade server-side auth
detail: Client builds a sign-in link with queryObj {ignoreOtp:true} ('/' + '?ignoreOtp=true') and preauth logic branches on URL params (w, sa, LoginRedir). If the server honors a client-supplied ignoreOtp flag to skip the OTP step, that is an authentication bypass. Requires manual verification: the parameter existing client-side proves nothing about server behavior.
evidence: signin.f7b86212.js: 'x=z({url:"/",queryObj:{ignoreOtp:!0}})' used as the sign-in href; preauth branch checks 'a.w||a.sa||...a.LoginRedir'.

title: OTP challenge returns mobile_number (even on error path); client displays it
detail: POST /rest/users/otp/challenge {username, referral} returns {mobile_number, mobile_number_verified}. The client renders 'A text message with a passcode was sent to %s' with the raw value. The catch block also reads mobile_number from t.errors[0]. No client-side masking was found. If the server sends the number unmasked, anyone knowing a username learns the victim's phone number. Needs manual check of actual masking.
evidence: signin.f7b86212.js: '{mobile_number:t,mobile_number_verified:a}=e' then '"A text message with a passcode was sent to %s.",[r]'; error path: 'const{mobile_number:a,mobile_number_verified:s}=(...t.errors[0])||{}'

title: Unauthenticated preauth endpoint reveals account auth configuration
detail: POST /rest/users/preauth {username, referral} requires no authentication and returns {otp, type, redirectUrl}, which fully determines the login UX (OTP vs password vs redirect vs SSO). This is an auth-type oracle per username. Caveat: adjacent to program-excluded 'user enumeration' — value depends on whether auth-type disclosure is treated distinctly.
evidence: signin.f7b86212.js: 'I.A.post("/rest/users/preauth",{username:t,referral:a})' then '{otp:t,type:a,redirectUrl:s}=e||{}' drives all branching.

title: ToS gate is client-side UI; access token is issued BEFORE ToS acceptance
detail: Login returns {tos_required, access_token, redirectUrl}. The client then GETs /rest/users/me/tos with the Bearer token, shows a checkbox (Accept button disabled until checked - pure UI gate), and POSTs {referral, accept:"true"} (string). Two server-side questions: (1) is the pre-ToS access token scoped to nothing-but-ToS, and (2) does the server strictly validate accept==="true" vs truthy. Client enforces nothing here.
evidence: signin.f7b86212.js: 'I.A.post("/rest/users/me/tos",{referral:t,accept:"true"},{headers:{Authorization:"Bearer ".concat(a)}})'; button 'disabled:!N' where N=checkbox state.

title: Password complexity enforced server-side (no client/server gap found)
detail: Password rules surface only as server error codes mapped to UI strings (ERR_INPUT_PASSWORD_COMPLEXITY_ERROR, PASSWORD_HISTORY_ERROR, PASSWORD_COMPLEXITY_ERROR_UNICODE, PASSWORD_INVALID_ERROR). No client-side password regex found. This is the correct pattern - nothing to exploit here.
evidence: signin.f7b86212.js error-code map: ERR_INPUT_PASSWORD_COMPLEXITY_ERROR:(...)'Your new password does not meet the password complexity requirements'

title: Auth REST surface enumerated from signin bundle
detail: Client-discovered endpoints: POST /rest/users/actions/login, POST /rest/users/preauth, POST /rest/users/otp/challenge, POST /rest/users/otp/auth, POST /rest/users/otp/wrongNumber, GET+POST /rest/users/me/tos, GET+POST /rest/users/me/webauthn/authentication. Plus page routes /forgotPassword, /register. All take a client-supplied 'referral' parameter.
evidence: signin.f7b86212.js static strings; every auth POST includes {referral}.

title: disclaimer rendered via dangerouslySetInnerHTML through sanitizer N.pn
detail: ToS disclaimer HTML is rendered with dangerouslySetInnerHTML after passing through (0,N.pn)(t,s). If N.pn is DOMPurify this is fine; if it is a hand-rolled sanitizer or identity function, stored-XSS via ToS text is possible. Could not resolve the minified import statically - flagged for manual follow-up.
